subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Common Pool Resource Dilemma
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Common Pool Resource Dilemma.

hook.text: Fishermen overfished the Grand Banks of Newfoundland until the cod collapsed in 1992.

buildup.text: Hardin called it the tragedy of the commons: shared resources get overused when individuals act in self-interest.

discovery.text: Ostrom won the Nobel Prize showing that communities can self-govern commons without privatization or government control.

twist.text: Her conditions: clear boundaries, shared rules, local monitoring, and graduated sanctions.

climax.text: The tragedy of the commons is not inevitable. With the right social institutions, shared resources can be sustained.

punchline.text: Commons fail without rules. Rules work without ownership.

quiz.question: What did Elinor Ostrom demonstrate about commons?
options: They must always be privatized to be sustained
Communities can self-govern shared resources with the right institutions
Government control is the only solution

details.summary: Common pool resource dilemmas occur when individuals exploit shared resources like fisheries, forests, or groundwater for personal gain, depleting the resource for everyone. Each person's rational self-interest leads to collectively irrational destruction.
details.whyItMatters: Overfishing, deforestation, and water depletion are all common pool resource tragedies. Elinor Ostrom won the Nobel Prize for showing that communities can manage commons successfully through social norms rather than just regulation or privatization.
takeaways: Individual rational exploitation destroys shared resources collectively
Ostrom showed communities can self-govern commons through norms and rules
Social trust and monitoring are key to sustainable shared resource management

faq.question: What is Ostrom's solution to the tragedy of the commons?
faq.answer: Elinor Ostrom documented communities worldwide that successfully manage shared resources without government control or privatization. Key ingredients include clear boundaries, local rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and collective decision making.

faq.question: Why do people overexploit shared resources?
faq.answer: Each individual captures the full benefit of taking more but bears only a fraction of the cost, which is shared by all users. Without social norms or rules limiting extraction, the rational individual choice is to take as much as possible.
